function.name: cronjob
function.description:
Manage scheduled cron jobs with a single compressed tool.

Use action='create' to schedule a new job from a prompt or one or more skills.
Use action='list' to inspect jobs.
Use action='update', 'pause', 'resume', 'remove', or 'run' to manage an existing job.

To stop a job the user no longer wants: first action='list' to find the job_id, then action='remove' with that job_id. Never guess job IDs — always list first.

Jobs run in a fresh session with no current-chat context, so prompts must be self-contained.
If skills are provided on create, the future cron run loads those skills in order, then follows the prompt as the task instruction.
On update, passing skills=[] clears attached skills.

NOTE: The agent's final response is auto-delivered to the target. Put the primary
user-facing content in the final response. Cron jobs run autonomously with no user
present — they cannot ask questions or request clarification.

Important safety rule: cron-run sessions should not recursively schedule more cron jobs.

action.description: One of: create, list, update, pause, resume, remove, run

prompt.description: For create: the full self-contained prompt. If skills are also provided, this becomes the task instruction paired with those skills.

repeat.description: Optional repeat count. Omit for defaults (once for one-shot, forever for recurring).

deliver.description: Omit this parameter to auto-deliver back to the current chat and topic (recommended). Auto-detection preserves thread/topic context. Only set explicitly when the user asks to deliver somewhere OTHER than the current conversation. Values: 'origin' (same as omitting), 'local' (no delivery, save only), or platform:chat_id:thread_id for a specific destination. Examples: 'telegram:-1001234567890:17585', 'discord:#engineering', 'sms:+15551234567'. WARNING: 'platform:chat_id' without :thread_id loses topic targeting.

skills.description: Optional ordered list of skill names to load before executing the cron prompt. On update, pass an empty array to clear attached skills.

model.description: Optional per-job model override. If provider is omitted, the current main provider is pinned at creation time so the job stays stable.

provider.description: Provider name (e.g. 'openrouter', 'anthropic'). Omit to use and pin the current provider.

script.description: Optional path to a Python script that runs before each cron job execution. Its stdout is injected into the prompt as context. Use for data collection and change detection. Relative paths resolve under ~/.hermes/scripts/. On update, pass empty string to clear.

context_from.description: Optional job ID or list of job IDs whose most recent completed output is injected into the prompt as context before each run. Use this to chain cron jobs: job A collects data, job B processes it. Each entry must be a valid job ID (from cronjob action='list'). Note: injects the most recent completed output — does not wait for upstream jobs running in the same tick. On update, pass an empty array to clear.

enabled_toolsets.description: Optional list of toolset names to restrict the job's agent to (e.g. ["web", "terminal", "file", "delegation"]). When set, only tools from these toolsets are loaded, significantly reducing input token overhead. When omitted, all default tools are loaded. Infer from the job's prompt — e.g. use "web" if it calls web_search, "terminal" if it runs scripts, "file" if it reads files, "delegation" if it calls delegate_task. On update, pass an empty array to clear.

workdir.description: Optional absolute path to run the job from. When set, AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules from that directory are injected into the system prompt, and the terminal/file/code_exec tools use it as their working directory — useful for running a job inside a specific project repo. Must be an absolute path that exists. When unset (default), preserves the original behaviour: no project context files, tools use the scheduler's cwd. On update, pass an empty string to clear. Jobs with workdir run sequentially (not parallel) to keep per-job directories isolated.

target.description: Delivery target. Format: 'platform' (uses home channel), 'platform:#channel-name', 'platform:chat_id', or 'platform:chat_id:thread_id' for Telegram topics and Discord threads. Examples: 'telegram', 'telegram:-1001234567890:17585', 'discord:999888777:555444333', 'discord:#bot-home', 'slack:#engineering', 'signal:+155****4567', 'matrix:!roomid:server.org', 'matrix:@user:server.org'

function.name: session_search
function.description:
Search your long-term memory of past conversations, or browse recent sessions. This is your recall -- every past session is searchable, and this tool summarizes what happened.

TWO MODES:
1. Recent sessions (no query): Call with no arguments to see what was worked on recently. Returns titles, previews, and timestamps. Zero LLM cost, instant. Start here when the user asks what were we working on or what did we do recently.
2. Keyword search (with query): Search for specific topics across all past sessions. Returns LLM-generated summaries of matching sessions.

USE THIS PROACTIVELY when:
- The user says 'we did this before', 'remember when', 'last time', 'as I mentioned'
- The user asks about a topic you worked on before but don't have in current context
- The user references a project, person, or concept that seems familiar but isn't in memory
- You want to check if you've solved a similar problem before
- The user asks 'what did we do about X?' or 'how did we fix Y?'

Don't hesitate to search when it is actually cross-session -- it's fast and cheap. Better to search and confirm than to guess or ask the user to repeat themselves.

Search syntax: keywords joined with OR for broad recall (elevenlabs OR baseten OR funding), phrases for exact match ("docker networking"), boolean (python NOT java), prefix (deploy*). IMPORTANT: Use OR between keywords for best results — FTS5 defaults to AND which misses sessions that only mention some terms. If a broad OR query returns nothing, try individual keyword searches in parallel. Returns summaries of the top matching sessions.

query.description: Search query — keywords, phrases, or boolean expressions to find in past sessions. Omit this parameter entirely to browse recent sessions instead (returns titles, previews, timestamps with no LLM cost).

role_filter.description: Optional: only search messages from specific roles (comma-separated). E.g. 'user,assistant' to skip tool outputs.

function.name: skill_manage
function.description:
Manage skills (create, update, delete). Skills are your procedural memory — reusable approaches for recurring task types. New skills go to ~/.hermes/skills/; existing skills can be modified wherever they live.

Actions: create (full SKILL.md + optional category), patch (old_string/new_string — preferred for fixes), edit (full SKILL.md rewrite — major overhauls only), delete, write_file, remove_file.

Create when: complex task succeeded (5+ calls), errors overcome, user-corrected approach worked, non-trivial workflow discovered, or user asks you to remember a procedure.
Update when: instructions stale/wrong, OS-specific failures, missing steps or pitfalls found during use. If you used a skill and hit issues not covered by it, patch it immediately.

After difficult/iterative tasks, offer to save as a skill. Skip for simple one-offs. Confirm with user before creating/deleting.

Good skills: trigger conditions, numbered steps with exact commands, pitfalls section, verification steps. Use skill_view() to see format examples.

name.description: Skill name (lowercase, hyphens/underscores, max 64 chars). Must match an existing skill for patch/edit/delete/write_file/remove_file.

content.description: Full SKILL.md content (YAML frontmatter + markdown body). Required for 'create' and 'edit'. For 'edit', read the skill first with skill_view() and provide the complete updated text.

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'patch'). Must be unique unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'patch'). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: For 'patch': replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false).

category.description: Optional category/domain for organizing the skill (e.g., 'devops', 'data-science', 'mlops'). Creates a subdirectory grouping. Only used with 'create'.

file_path.description: Path to a supporting file within the skill directory. For 'write_file'/'remove_file': required, must be under references/, templates/, scripts/, or assets/. For 'patch': optional, defaults to SKILL.md if omitted.

file_content.description: Content for the file. Required for 'write_file'.

function.name: skill_view
function.description: Skills allow for loading information about specific tasks and workflows, as well as scripts and templates. Load a skill's full content or access its linked files (references, templates, scripts). First call returns SKILL.md content plus a 'linked_files' dict showing available references/templates/scripts. To access those, call again with file_path parameter.

name.description: The skill name (use skills_list to see available skills). For plugin-provided skills, use the qualified form 'plugin:skill' (e.g. 'superpowers:writing-plans').

file_path.description: OPTIONAL: Path to a linked file within the skill (e.g., 'references/api.md', 'templates/config.yaml', 'scripts/validate.py'). Omit to get the main SKILL.md content.

function.name: skills_list
function.description: List available skills (name + description). Use skill_view(name) to load full content.

category.description: Optional category filter to narrow results

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

function.name: text_to_speech
function.description: Convert text to speech audio. Returns a MEDIA: path that the platform delivers as a voice message. On Telegram it plays as a voice bubble, on Discord/WhatsApp as an audio attachment. In CLI mode, saves to ~/voice-memos/. Voice and provider are user-configured, not model-selected.

text.description: The text to convert to speech. Provider-specific character caps apply and are enforced automatically (OpenAI 4096, xAI 15000, MiniMax 10000, ElevenLabs 5k-40k depending on model); over-long input is truncated.

output_path.description: Optional custom file path to save the audio. Defaults to ~/.hermes/audio_cache/<timestamp>.mp3

function.name: todo
function.description:
Manage your task list for the current session. Use for complex tasks with 3+ steps or when the user provides multiple tasks. Call with no parameters to read the current list.

Writing:
- Provide 'todos' array to create/update items
- merge=false (default): replace the entire list with a fresh plan
- merge=true: update existing items by id, add any new ones

Each item: {id: string, content: string, status: pending|in_progress|completed|cancelled}
List order is priority. Only ONE item in_progress at a time.
Mark items completed immediately when done. If something fails, cancel it and add a revised item.

Always returns the full current list.

todos.description: Task items to write. Omit to read current list.

merge.description: true: update existing items by id, add new ones. false (default): replace the entire list.

function.name: vision_analyze
function.description: Analyze images using AI vision. Provides a comprehensive description and answers a specific question about the image content.

image_url.description: Image URL (http/https) or local file path to analyze.

question.description: Your specific question or request about the image to resolve. The AI will automatically provide a complete image description AND answer your specific question.

function.name: web_extract
function.description: Extract content from web page URLs. Returns page content in markdown format. Also works with PDF URLs (arxiv papers, documents, etc.) — pass the PDF link directly and it converts to markdown text. Pages under 5000 chars return full markdown; larger pages are LLM-summarized and capped at ~5000 chars per page. Pages over 2M chars are refused. If a URL fails or times out, use the browser tool to access it instead.

urls.description: List of URLs to extract content from (max 5 URLs per call)

function.name: web_search
function.description: Search the web for information on any topic. Returns up to 5 relevant results with titles, URLs, and descriptions.

query.description: The search query to look up on the web

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 1 – The Descent Window
     2|
     3|Scene 1. Entry plasma washes the forward cameras white as Elena calls the descent profile. Mars is introduced not as a red postcard, but as thin air that is too weak to help much and too strong to ignore. Plain-language technical thread: Landing on Mars is hard because there is enough air to create heat and drag, but not enough to slow a heavy ship safely on its own.
     4|
     5|Scene 2. Arun monitors heat, pressure, and structural loads. He tells a frightened crewmate that the ship is being squeezed, shaken, and cooked all at once.
     6|
     7|Scene 3. Ship One lands hard. Dust blinds sensors. Elena refuses celebration until pressure holds.
     8|
     9|Scene 4. They learn Ship Two is safe and Ship Three is alive but tilted. Relief is immediate and incomplete.
    10|
    11|Scene 5. The three ships glow in the dark through drifting dust. Gabriel thinks they look less like explorers than survivors already. Bridge: The landing is only a victory if the cargo is intact.# Chapter 2 – Counting What Matters
    12|
    13|Scene 1. Jonah opens the cargo verification sequence. Not everything matters equally. He explains to a younger crewmate that on Mars, the difference between a luxury and a necessity is whether it keeps air in, water clean, or power flowing.
    14|
    15|Scene 2. Robots unload pressure tunnels, power converters, greenhouse pallets, machine tools, and water hardware.
    16|
    17|Scene 3. A damaged crate turns out to contain spare suit bearings. That one impact suddenly matters more than half a ton of comfort items. Plain-language technical thread: A colony does not fail because it lacks cool equipment. It fails because tiny wear parts run out.
    18|
    19|Scene 4. Mei opens seed storage and growth trays. She feels hope and dread in the same moment.
    20|
    21|Scene 5. Elena orders full inventory triage by survival class. Bridge: To know what they can survive, they first need a livable base.# Chapter 3 – Making Air Between Ships
    22|
    23|Scene 1. The crews connect the first flexible tunnel between two ships. The act feels like stitching wounds together.
    24|
    25|Scene 2. Arun explains pressure simply to Gabriel: outside, Mars air is too thin to keep liquid water stable in the open, so the base is really a bubble of borrowed Earth.
    26|
    27|Scene 3. A coupling seal misaligns. For a few seconds, everyone watches a single red warning light decide the mood of the whole mission.
    28|
    29|Scene 4. The tunnel holds. A cheer breaks out because now people and supplies can move without suits.
    30|
    31|Scene 5. The third ship remains isolated longer because of its landing angle, creating the first subtle social split. Bridge: With the habitat linked, Earth should feel closer. Instead it starts to feel strange.# Chapter 4 – The Last Normal Messages
    32|
    33|Scene 1. Gabriel receives routine traffic from Earth: school recordings, agency praise, public excitement.
    34|
    35|Scene 2. Hidden inside the queue are delays, reroutes, and military priority flags.
    36|
    37|Scene 3. Elena chooses not to burden the whole crew yet.
    38|
    39|Scene 4. Over dinner, people talk about what they will do when they get home. Gabriel says little.
    40|
    41|Scene 5. The next scheduled packet does not arrive. Bridge: Silence becomes information.# Chapter 5 – Two-Year Thinking
    42|
    43|Scene 1. Elena briefs the original mission logic: two years on Mars, then return. Everything from food packaging to suit rotation assumed that timeline.
    44|
    45|Scene 2. Arun and Imani privately walk through what return actually means: launch vehicles, fuel chains, orbital assembly, crews on Earth, spare parts, politics. Plain-language technical thread: Rescue is not one rocket. Rescue is a whole civilization deciding to keep building one more bridge.
    46|
    47|Scene 3. Tomas hears enough to understand the danger.
    48|
    49|Scene 4. Elena records a private log admitting the mission may already be changing shape.
    50|
    51|Scene 5. Earth traffic remains broken. Bridge: They move from uncertainty to math.# Chapter 6 – Return Is a Supply Chain
    52|
    53|Scene 1. Arun lays out the numbers for Elena and Gabriel. No return ship means no return, regardless of bravery.
    54|
    55|Scene 2. Gabriel asks whether they should tell the crew now or wait for confirmation.
    56|
    57|Scene 3. Ship Three is finally stabilized and linked, but the mood is wrong for celebration.
    58|
    59|Scene 4. Elena visits the cargo bay and realizes most of it was packed for a temporary base, not a permanent town.
    60|
    61|Scene 5. She calls an all-hands meeting. Bridge: The colony is born the moment the truth is spoken aloud.# Chapter 7 – The Meeting No One Wanted
    62|
    63|Scene 1. Elena tells the crew Earth is unstable and return odds have sharply fallen.
    64|
    65|Scene 2. Nobody panics in a dramatic way. Instead the room fractures into anger, denial, bargaining, and technical questions.
    66|
    67|Scene 3. Laila asks the one question that matters: what changes right now.
    68|
    69|Scene 4. Elena says everything. EVA hours, food assumptions, maintenance cycles, power margins, experiment priorities.
    70|
    71|Scene 5. Gabriel begins the Founding Record because someone has to say when the old mission died. Bridge: The first test of the new reality comes from the planet itself.# Chapter 8 – Dust Weather
    72|
    73|Scene 1. Forecast models show rising dust. Imani says a dust storm on Mars is not like a hurricane pushing down walls; it is more like powder finding every weak point in every machine.
    74|
    75|Scene 2. Solar panels are braced. Exterior loaders keep working because there is no time to stop.
    76|
    77|Scene 3. Dust coats solar panels, optics, joints, and reactor radiators. A robot freezes in place with clogged movement rails.
    78|
    79|Scene 4. Power drops. Arun explains that dust is dangerous not because it is dramatic, but because it quietly lowers every margin at once.
    80|
    81|Scene 5. They survive the storm, but inspection shows the real damage has just begun. Bridge: To live here, they need local water before their imported reserves become a countdown.

    83|PART II – WATER, AIR, AND GROUND# Chapter 9 – Every Cup Twice
    84|
    85|Scene 1. Arun gives the first hard water briefing. On Mars, water is not only for drinking. It is for cleaning, cooling, crops, oxygen production, medicine, and industry.

    90|
    91|Scene 4. Tension rises in the mess hall when people realize showers are now engineering events.

    94|
    95|Scene 1. Imani leads a convoy with robots, drills, heaters, and sample gear.
    96|
    97|Scene 2. Gabriel rides along to document the search and learns how deceptive Mars ground can be. The surface can look uniform while hiding different layers below.
    98|

   105|Scene 1. The team returns with weak results. Some crew begin arguing that the landing site itself may have been a fatal compromise.
   106|
   107|Scene 2. Elena shuts down blame and orders a broader survey.
   108|
   109|Scene 3. Mei explains to Gabriel that good science can still produce bad outcomes when the question is survival.
   110|
   111|Scene 4. Tomas reassigns more robots to prospecting, angering Jonah, who needs them for habitat build-out.
   112|
   113|Scene 5. A second site lights up with stronger signatures. Bridge: They go back out with fewer illusions.# Chapter 12 – Dirty Water

   115|Scene 1. The second extraction reaches buried ice mixed with salts and soil fines.
   116|
   117|Scene 2. The first melted sample looks disgusting. Laila reminds everyone that ugly water can still become safe water if you have energy and patience. Plain-language technical thread: Water purification is less magic than stages—melt it, separate grit, strip bad chemistry, test it, then trust it.
   118|
   119|Scene 3. Arun worries about the energy cost more than the chemistry.
   120|
   121|Scene 4. They bring home the first batch for processing.
   122|
   123|Scene 5. Jonah paints LOCAL WATER on an empty tank before it is filled, as an act of faith. Bridge: Filling that tank becomes the next emotional target.# Chapter 13 – The First Tank
   124|
   125|Scene 1. Purification runs badly at first. Filters clog. Heating systems cycle wrong.
   126|
   127|Scene 2. Arun and Jonah improvise with industrial hardware not meant for this exact job.
   128|
   129|Scene 3. The tank finally begins to fill.
   130|
   131|Scene 4. No one cheers loudly. The sound of water hitting metal feels almost sacred.
   132|

   134|
   135|Scene 1. Arun reviews oxygen reserves and projected usage. They are safe for now, not safe forever.
   136|
   137|Scene 2. He explains Mars air simply: it is mostly carbon dioxide, which humans cannot breathe, but chemistry can split useful oxygen from it if you have machines and power.

   141|Scene 4. Jonah proposes scaling it up with repurposed compressors and heat systems.
   142|

   144|
   145|Scene 1. Jonah turns the machine shop into the heart of the colony. He explains to a new technician that a workshop on Mars is like a second circulatory system; if you cannot fix things, every other system starts bleeding out.
   146|
   147|Scene 2. Tomas assigns robots to assist with assembly.
   148|
   149|Scene 3. Mei objects when greenhouse labor is cut again.
   150|
   151|Scene 4. The crew works through the night in a mood halfway between invention and desperation.
   152|

   154|
   155|Scene 1. The enlarged oxygen train is powered up.
   156|
   157|Scene 2. Heat rises too fast. Alarms trip. For a moment it looks like the whole thing will cook itself.
   158|
   159|Scene 3. Arun explains under pressure that many machines fail the same way people do—they get overwhelmed faster than they can shed what is hurting them.
   160|
   161|Scene 4. A manual bypass stabilizes the run.
   162|
   163|Scene 5. Reserve oxygen begins climbing. Bridge: Now that the base can breathe longer, Laila forces them to face what living there does to the body.

   166|
   167|Scene 1. Laila presents cumulative exposure models. Mars does not blast them all at once every day, but the dose builds quietly over time.
   168|
   169|Scene 2. She explains radiation in plain language as invisible damage that the body can sometimes repair and sometimes cannot.
   170|
   171|Scene 3. The imported habitat modules are strong enough to hold pressure, not massive enough to shield years of exposure safely.

"Let me tell you what twelve percent means," she said. "It means three trays of leafy greens. It means maybe half a tray of microgreens. It means the experiment I have running on soy germination will fail because I cannot give the starter trays enough moisture to establish roots."

She took a step forward.

"Twelve percent means we eat packaged food forever. It means we never get fresh calories. It means morale drops, nutrition degrades, and the body starts losing the war against itself because we could not spare an extra two liters a day for plants."

Arun did not look away.

"I understand," he said. "Show me where to take the two liters from. Hygiene? Cooling? Drinking? Pick one."

"I pick efficiency improvements in your loop."

"There are no efficiency improvements I have not already found."

"Then find better ones."

"I have been doing this for eighteen years, Mei. I know the limits of the hardware."

"Then the hardware needs to change."

They stared at each other. The frozen video link flickered. Somewhere in Ship Three, a colonist who could not see their faces heard the silence and must have wondered if the connection had dropped.

Elena, sitting in the front row with her arms crossed, let the silence hold for a few more seconds before she said, "We will revisit the allocation when we have better numbers from the next water survey. Until then, the greenhouse gets twelve percent."

Mei sat down. She did not look satisfied. She looked like someone who had just been told her children would eat less so the adults could breathe.

---

After the briefing, Arun stayed in the common room to answer questions. Most were technical. Filter change intervals. Pump redundancy. Chemical dosing schedules.

Gabriel, the archivist, waited until the others left. He pulled up a chair and sat across from Arun.

"Walk me through the loop again," he said. "For the record. In plain language."

Arun rubbed his eyes. He was tired. He was always tired now.

"Okay," he said. "The simple version."

He picked up the plastic cup. Still half full.

"You drink this. Your body processes it. Some goes out as sweat. Some goes out as urine. Some goes out as vapor in your breath."

He set the cup down.

"The air handler collects the vapor. Condenses it. Pumps it to the skid. The toilet collects the urine and solids. The urine goes to the skid too. The solids go to a digester that breaks them down into fertilizer and more water. The shower drain goes to the skid. The kitchen sink goes to the skid."

He drew an invisible circle with his finger.

"The skid has three stages. First, particulate filtration. It catches hair, lint, food scraps, anything solid. Second, activated carbon. It pulls out organic compounds, odors, discoloration. Third, reverse osmosis. It forces water through a membrane at high pressure. The membrane blocks salts, metals, microbes, viruses. Everything except pure H₂O."

"And after RO?"

"After RO, we add back trace minerals for health and taste. Then we run it through a UV sterilizer as insurance. Then it goes into the clean tank. Ready to drink."

Gabriel wrote that down. He was meticulous. Arun respected that.

"What happens to the waste from the filtration?" Gabriel said.

"It gets concentrated. Brine, mostly. We store it in tanks. Eventually we process it further to recover the last usable water. After that, the solids are dried and stored."

"Stored where?"

"In a sealed container near the power plant. It is not hazardous. It is just useless."

Gabriel wrote something else. Then he looked up.

"One hundred and forty-three days," he said. "That number assumes nominal consumption. What is nominal?"

"Two point five liters per person per day for drinking and food prep. Five for hygiene. Four for cooling loops. Three for crop allocation. One for cleaning and miscellaneous."

"Sixteen and a half liters per person per day. Total."

"Yes."

"And we are actually using more than that."

"We are using eighteen. Because the cooling loop is running hot and the crops are thirsty and people are scared and taking slightly longer showers than they should."

Gabriel nodded. He did not argue. He just wrote.

---

The recycling skid was housed in a separate module connected to the main habitat by a short tunnel. It was loud. Pumps throbbed. Valves clicked. Water moved through pipes with a sound like breathing.

Arun visited it four times a day. Sometimes five. He checked pressure readings, flow rates, conductivity sensors. He calibrated the dosing pumps for the mineral injection stage. He swabbed the UV chamber window to keep the sensor clean.

The machine was his responsibility. He had helped design its predecessor for a polar research station in Antarctica. The Mars version was smaller, lighter, more automated, and less forgiving. Antarctica had a supply chain. Antarctica had rescue. Antarctica had air you could breathe if you opened a door.

Mars had none of those things.

He pulled the inspection panel off the RO pump and checked the seals. They looked good. He checked the membrane pressure. Slightly high. He adjusted the bypass valve and watched the gauge settle.

Every adjustment was a compromise. Higher pressure meant more recovery but faster membrane degradation. Lower pressure meant gentler on the hardware but worse water quality. There was no perfect setting. There was only the least bad one for the current conditions.

He closed the panel and wiped his hands on a rag.

The skid had been running for six weeks. In that time, it had processed approximately eighteen thousand liters of water. Every drop had come from somewhere inside the habitat. Every drop had been dirty. Every drop had been cleaned.

Eighty-eight percent recovery now. Not ninety-two. The difference was three hundred liters lost to the brine tanks. Three hundred liters that Mei could have used for her soy germination trays.

Arun had not told anyone that number. He would tell Elena tonight. Then they would decide what to do about it.

---

The mess hall that evening was subdued. People ate their packaged meals in small groups. The conversation was quiet, the laughter thin.

Tomas, the robotics engineer, sat with Jonah, the mechanic. They were arguing about filter clog rates in low gravity. It was not an argument. It was two people who needed to talk about something technical so they did not have to talk about the briefing.

Imani sat alone with a tablet, scrolling through survey data. She was the geologist. She had been quiet since the briefing ended.

Arun walked past her table. She looked up.

"You have a minute?" she said.

He sat down.

"I have been looking at the orbital survey data," she said. "There is a formation forty kilometers northwest of here. The spectral signature suggests buried ice at a depth of three to five meters. Shallow enough to access with our drills. Thick enough to matter."

"How thick?"

"At least ten meters. Possibly more."

Arun considered that. Ten meters of ice was a lot of water. Enough to top up the reserves for months. Enough to bring the recovery margin back to comfortable.

"What is the catch?" he said.

"Forty kilometers is a multi-day trip. We would need a convoy. Support vehicles. Full habitation support. The survey took three passes and the readings are good but they are not perfect. There could be less ice than I think. There could be more rocks. There could be terrain problems the orbital imagery does not show."

"You want to go."

"I want to propose it formally. To Elena. Tomorrow."

"She will ask about the risk."

"I will tell her the truth. The risk is real. The reward is a water reserve that changes the math of this colony for a year or more."

Arun looked at the table. At the condensation rings from a water bottle. At the micro-scratches in the laminate. At the tiny details of a surface he had seen a thousand times.

"It is going to be hard to argue against," he said.

"It is going to be hard to argue for," she said. "If the ice is not there, or if it is too salty to process, or if the convoy runs into trouble, we lose equipment we cannot replace and we lose time we do not have."

"And if we do not go?"

"Then we stay in the hundred-and-forty-three-day window forever. Living on recycled sweat and counting the days until the math stops working."

Arun nodded. He understood that kind of math. He lived inside it.

"Talk to Elena in the morning," he said. "I will back you on the technical feasibility."

Imani smiled. It was not a happy smile. It was the smile of someone who had just volunteered for a dangerous job and was still deciding whether that made her brave or stupid.

---

Later that night, Arun walked through the habitat on his final check. The lights were dimmed to conserve power. The corridors were empty.

He stopped at the hygiene module. A small room with a shower head, a sink, and a toilet. All of it connected to the skid. All of it part of the loop.

The shower had a timer. Three minutes. That was the allocation. Three minutes per person every other day. The timer was bolted to the wall and wired into the water valve. When it hit zero, the valve closed.

Arun had installed it himself. He had hated doing it. He hated that a timer was necessary.

He remembered his first shower on Mars. After the dust storm. After the landing. After three days in a suit. He had stood under the spray for five minutes. Maybe six. The water had been warm and plentiful and he had not thought about it at all.

He would never do that again.

He touched the timer. Plastic. Cheap. Mechanical. It ticked quietly in the dark.

Three minutes. Every other day. And if the skid lost another percentage point, it would be two minutes. And if the ice search failed, it would be one. And if the loop broke completely, it would be zero.

He walked back to his bunk. The pipes hummed in the walls. Water moving. The base's circulatory system. The only thing standing between thirty people and a slow death by dehydration.

He lay down and stared at the ceiling.

In the morning, Imani would propose the ice search. Mei would demand more water for the greenhouse. Elena would balance the demands of the hungry against the needs of the thirsty.

Arun would check the skid. Calibrate the sensors. Adjust the bypass valve. And maybe, if he was lucky, the numbers would hold for one more day.

That was the job.

Water on Mars was not magic. It was work. It was measurement and maintenance and hard choices made by tired people in a metal box a hundred million kilometers from home.

Every cup twice.

Every drop counted.

Every day a gift they had to earn.
"}
